904.title: The Dome of the Rock
904.hook: a golden dome in Jerusalem over the rock linked with the night journey
904.howItsDone: Muslims visiting Jerusalem pray at al-Aqsa Mosque and visit the Dome of the Rock on the same plaza, and the night journey is remembered on the night Muslims call al-Isra wal-Mi'raj.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Damascus, one ruling house from the Atlantic to the Indus. Your line was from spain to sindh.

Inside, the light drops. You come in from the bright stone plaza, and your eyes adjust. Columns of marble. Gold mosaic catching what light there is. And in the middle, behind a railing, not a floor at all but a great bare outcrop of rock, rough and uneven, the hill itself coming up through the building. Everything else was built around it. Above it, the dome. This is Jerusalem, on the high plaza Muslims call al-Haram al-Sharif, the Noble Sanctuary. Today: the Dome of the Rock.

Start with the journey. The Qur'an opens one surah with it: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship." The Inviolable Place is the Kaaba in Mecca. The Far Distant Place, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, is understood in Islamic tradition as Jerusalem. The hadith collections tell how, from there, the Prophet ﷺ was taken up through the heavens, and tradition links that ascent with this rock. The rock is holy in Jewish tradition too, on the hill where the Temple stood. Now the building. Tradition says the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik had it raised over the rock. Its plan is an octagon, with rings of columns, so pilgrims can walk around the rock beneath the dome. One distinction: the Dome of the Rock is not the mosque. It's a shrine. The mosque for congregational prayer, al-Aqsa Mosque, stands at the southern end of the same plaza. Look up inside and a long band of Arabic runs around the walls in gold mosaic: verses of the Qur'an, including verses about Jesus son of Mary, whom the Qur'an honors as a messenger. Outside, the walls blaze with blue and white tiles, added in a later age, so the building has been dressed by more than one generation. A city holy to many, a journey by night, and over the spot, a dome over the rock.
screen: then, large: `A DOME OVER THE ROCK.`

segments.voice: If you can, look at a close photo of the outer tiles and follow one line of the pattern until it turns and meets itself, noticing the writing woven into the design. Then close your eyes and picture the rock inside, untouched, with the whole building shaped around it. If you pray, you can recite the opening of Surah al-Isra: glorified be He who carried His servant by night.
Sakhrah, the rock itself: the bare stone at the center of the shrine, linked in tradition with the Prophet's night journey and holy in Jewish tradition too. Today's word.
Your line: a dome over the rock. Built around it, not over it. That's day nine hundred four.

905.title: The Umayyad Mosque
905.hook: the great mosque of Damascus, built on a site holy for centuries, still has a shrine honoring Yahya (John the Baptist)
905.howItsDone: Worshipers at the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus pray in its great hall and visit the shrine honoring Yahya (John the Baptist), which Christian visitors also come to.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sakhrah, the rock under the dome in Jerusalem. Your line was a dome over the rock.

In the prayer hall of the great mosque of Damascus, among the carpets and the columns, stands a small domed shrine behind a grille. People stop at it. Some touch the grille. Some pray beside it. Christians come to it too. It honors a prophet the Qur'an calls Yahya, and Christians call John the Baptist. Tradition says his head is buried there. A shrine to John inside a mosque, in the old capital of the caliphs. Today: the Umayyad Mosque.

Start with the ground under it. The histories describe this site as holy before Islam: a temple in Roman times, and later a church dedicated to John the Baptist. Later histories report that after the Muslims came to Damascus, for a time Muslims and Christians both prayed on the site. Then the Umayyad caliph al-Walid, son of Abd al-Malik, built the great mosque here, reusing the old walls. So the mosque stands on layer upon layer of prayer. And it kept John. The Qur'an tells Yahya's story with warmth: "Peace on him the day he was born, and the day he dieth and the day he shall be raised alive!" Another layer looks forward. One of the mosque's minarets is called the Minaret of Jesus. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says that Jesus son of Mary will descend near a white minaret east of Damascus, and tradition links that report to this tower. So one building holds a Roman past, a Christian past, a Muslim present, and a hope about the end of days. Then the courtyard, wide and open, and the gold mosaics of trees, rivers and houses on its walls, which some readers see as a picture of paradise. Old stone, many prayers, one place. Layers of holiness.

Bring the courtyard to mind: wide stone, open sky, pigeons, minarets above, and around it a very old city, home to families of more than one faith, that has lived through hard years. If you pray, ask God for peace on Damascus and its people, in your own words or in silence. If you don't, hold the city in mind with goodwill, one breath at a time.
Yahya, the Qur'an's name for John the Baptist: the prophet honored with a shrine inside the great mosque of Damascus, built on layer upon layer of older prayer. Today's word.
Your line: layers of holiness. One place, prayed in again and again. Day nine hundred five, done.

906.title: Arabic coins and offices
906.hook: Arabic becomes the language of government, and coins carry verses instead of faces
906.howItsDone: Historians and coin collectors study the Umayyad reform dinars, which carry the declaration of God's oneness and verses from Surah al-Ikhlas, and al-Ikhlas is a surah recited in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yahya, John the Baptist, honored inside the Umayyad Mosque. Your line was layers of holiness.

Turn a coin over in your hand. There may be a face on it: a president, a queen, a national hero. Putting a ruler's face on money is an old habit. In the early Umayyad years, Muslim mints did much the same, striking coins in the old styles of the empires before them, with crowned figures and portraits, sometimes with a few Arabic words added at the edge. Then the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik changed the gold and the silver. The faces went. In their place: nothing but words. Today: Arabic coins and offices.

Look at one of the new gold coins, the dinar. In Arabic script it says: there is no god but God, alone, without partner. Around it, words from the Qur'an. One side carries most of a short surah, al-Ikhlas, without its opening command, say, and without its last line. In Pickthall's translation, the words on the coin read: "He is Allah, the One! Allah, the eternally Besought of all! He begetteth not nor was begotten." A coin travels, through markets and purses from one end of the map to the other. Now it carried, not a ruler's face, but a statement about God. The same change came to the offices. Three days ago, the clerks kept the registers in Greek in Syria and in Persian in Iraq. The historian al-Baladhuri reports that under Abd al-Malik the registers of Syria were moved into Arabic, and under his governor al-Hajjaj the registers of Iraq were moved from Persian. Arabic became the language of tax rolls, letters and records. That's how a language of poetry and revelation also became a language of paperwork. Two small reforms, a coin and a ledger, changed what the money looked like and how the offices wrote. Words instead of faces.

If there's a coin nearby, pick it up, ignore the picture, and read every word on it slowly, front and back, noticing what its makers chose to say to everyone who would ever hold it. Then set it down and close your eyes. If you pray, you can recite Surah al-Ikhlas, the words those gold coins carried; if not, simply hold the coin's words in mind.
Dinar, the gold coin of the caliphs: reformed by Abd al-Malik to carry words of faith instead of a ruler's face, alongside registers of empire moved into Arabic. Today's word.
Your line: words instead of faces. A coin can carry a creed across a whole map. See you tomorrow.

907.title: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz
907.hook: a caliph of the ruling family who began his reforms with his own family's wealth
907.howItsDone: Muslims often tell stories of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, such as the two lamps, when they talk about honest leadership and keeping public money apart from private use.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dinar, words where a face had been. Your line was words instead of faces.

A lamp is burning on a desk in Damascus. A visitor comes in, and once the state's business is done, the talk turns to family news. The man at the desk reaches over, puts the lamp out, and lights a different one. The first lamp, he explains, burns oil paid for by the public treasury. This conversation is his own, so it gets his own lamp. That's a story people tell about Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, an Umayyad caliph. Whether or not it happened just that way, it shows what people remembered: a ruler who kept careful track of what was his and what belonged to everyone. Today: the caliph they called just.
screen: `A LAMP ON A DESK.` → `PUT OUT FOR A PRIVATE TALK.` → `WHAT IS MINE, WHAT IS EVERYONE'S.`

segments.voice: Start with another story people tell: the girl and the milk. The caliph Umar ibn al-Khattab is walking Medina by night. Through a wall he hears a mother tell her daughter to stretch the milk with water before selling it. The daughter says the caliph has forbidden that. The mother says the caliph can't see them. And the girl answers: if Umar does not see, the Lord of Umar sees. The story says Umar married her to his son. Her daughter's son was Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz. So he is the just grandson: the girl who wouldn't cheat in the dark was his grandmother, and the caliph who heard her was his forebear. Now the man himself. Born into the ruling family and raised in comfort, he was, the histories say, governor of Medina before he became caliph. When he took power, the reports say he started with his own house, returning lands and goods his family had taken unjustly, beginning with what he held himself. His wife Fatima, a caliph's daughter, is reported to have given her jewels to the treasury. He also ended something ugly. Under earlier Umayyad rulers, Ali ibn Abi Talib had been cursed from the pulpits. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz stopped it, and the reports say the Friday sermon came to close with a verse instead, the one that begins, in Pickthall's translation, "Lo! Allah enjoineth justice and kindness." His rule was short. But some Sunni scholars later counted him with the rightly guided caliphs, calling him the fifth.

segments.voice: Picture the two lamps on the desk, and name one thing in your life that is more than you need: a subscription, a second helping, an extra hour on a screen. If you pray, ask for contentment in your own words; if you don't, rest with the question of what is enough.
Umar. The Umayyad caliph remembered for justice and simple living, who returned what his own family had taken and ended the cursing from the pulpits. Today's word.

908.title: Hasan al-Basri
908.hook: the preacher of Basra who warned rulers and taught inner watchfulness
908.howItsDone: Some Muslims practice muhasaba, taking stock of the day's words and deeds, for example at night before sleep, and Sufi teachers describe muraqaba, watchfulness, as a discipline of the heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, who returned what his own family had taken. Your line was the just grandson.

Basra, a city in southern Iraq. In its mosque, an old man sits with a circle of listeners around him. He is not a ruler or a general. He holds no office. The biographers describe him as a man who seemed always to be grieving, as if he had just come back from burying someone. When he speaks about death and the day of reckoning, people lean in, and some weep with him. Yet this quiet, sorrowful man would say hard things about a feared governor of his day. His name was al-Hasan, and because of the city, history calls him Hasan al-Basri. Today: the preacher who watched his own heart first.
screen: `A CIRCLE IN THE MOSQUE AT BASRA.` → `A MAN WHO SEEMED TO GRIEVE.` → `HARD WORDS FOR THE POWERFUL.`

segments.voice: His world was the Umayyad world of new cities, new wealth, new palaces. Iraq was governed by al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, a man the histories remember for his harshness. The reports say Hasan spoke against al-Hajjaj's cruelty, and at times had to hide from him. He didn't lead a revolt. When some urged him to join an armed rising, the reports say he refused. His fight was a different one. Hasan kept turning his listeners back toward their own hearts. One saying attributed to him runs something like this: son of Adam, you are nothing but days, and when a day goes, a part of you goes with it. Another says the believer is the one who holds himself to account. Later Muslim writers developed that idea into disciplines of the inner life: muhasaba, taking account of yourself, and muraqaba, watchfulness, living as one who is watched by God. They found its ground in the Qur'an, where God says He knows what a person's soul whispers, and is nearer to him than his jugular vein. For them, if God is that near, every thought is lived in company. Sufi writers count Hasan among their early teachers, and scholars of law and doctrine claim him too. A story told about the beginnings of the Mu'tazila school of theology even says it began when a student named Wasil ibn Ata left Hasan's circle over a disputed question. Many streams, the story suggests, flowed from one mosque in Basra.
screen: `AL-HAJJAJ AND THE HARSH YEARS.` · `NO REVOLT, BUT HARD WORDS.` · `YOU ARE NOTHING BUT DAYS.` · then, large: `WATCHFULNESS.`

segments.voice: Without changing anything, notice what is moving in you right now, a worry, a wish, a small irritation from this morning, and name each one quietly as it passes, the way someone on a riverbank might name the boats. Don't chase them and don't scold them; just watch. If you pray, you can remember that, in Hasan's tradition, you are not the only one watching.
Hasan al-Basri. The preacher of Basra who spoke against a harsh governor, refused to take up arms, and taught people to hold themselves to account. Today's word.
Your line: watch the heart. You are nothing but days, so each one counts. That's day nine hundred eight.

909.title: The seven jurists of Medina
909.hook: scholars of the city who kept the Prophet's practice
909.howItsDone: In the Maliki school of law, the practice of the people of Medina is weighed as evidence alongside the hadith, and students in other schools also learn hadith through chains of teachers that pass through Medina.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hasan al-Basri, the preacher who said we are nothing but days. Your line was watch the heart.

Where do you go to learn how the Prophet prayed, once the people who prayed beside him are gone? Books help. But a book can't show you how a hand is raised, or how long a pause is held. For that, people went to a place. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, had lived in Medina, and Medina remembered. The children and grandchildren of his Companions grew up on its streets, in the houses where he had eaten and taught. In the Umayyad years, while Damascus held the government, Medina held something else. Its scholars became famous as a group: the seven jurists of Medina. Today: the city that kept the practice.
screen: `HOW DID HE PRAY?` → `A BOOK CAN'T SHOW A PAUSE.` → `MEDINA REMEMBERED.`

segments.voice: These men belonged to the generation Muslims call the Followers, the ones who learned from the Companions. Their names tell the story. Urwa ibn al-Zubayr was a nephew of Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and passed on a great deal of what she taught. Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad was a grandson of Abu Bakr and, the reports say, grew up in Aisha's care. Kharija was a son of Zayd ibn Thabit, the Companion who wrote down revelation for the Prophet. And Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, the biographers say, was sought out for his learning on hard questions. Each stood one step from the Companions themselves. One wrinkle: the lists agree on most of the names, but differ over the seventh. A famous group, and its membership is still debated. What did they do? They answered questions. How do you divide an inheritance? What does a fair sale look like? They answered from what the Companions had said and done, and from what Medina still did. When Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz governed the city, the reports say he called its jurists together and promised to act on nothing without their counsel. A later Medinan scholar, Malik ibn Anas, made this a principle: the practice of the people of Medina. For him, what a whole city had done since the Prophet's day was itself a kind of witness. Medina became the city of the practice.
screen: `THE FOLLOWERS OF THE COMPANIONS.` · `ONE STEP FROM THE COMPANIONS.` · `SIX AGREED, THE SEVENTH DEBATED.` · then, large: `THE PRACTICE OF MEDINA.`

Sit with that picture for a few breaths, a man whose words shaped a city helping at home, and bring to mind one small task in your own home that someone else usually does.

910.title: To Spain and Sindh
910.hook: Umayyad armies reach both Spain and the Indus, and a new world opens
910.howItsDone: Muslims in Spain, Pakistan and India today sometimes trace their communities' stories back to these early arrivals, and historians read al-Baladhuri and other chronicles to reconstruct them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seven jurists of Medina, answering from what the city remembered. Your line was the city of the practice.

Boats push off from the North African shore and cross the narrow strait into Spain. Far to the east, troops march into Sindh, the lower Indus valley, in what is now Pakistan. Two armies at opposite ends of one empire ruled from Damascus, sent out by different governors, in the same few years. The histories date the crossing into Spain to the year ninety-two after the Hijra, which in the Christian calendar is 711. Today: to Spain and Sindh.
screen: `BOATS CROSS THE STRAIT.` → `TROOPS MARCH INTO SINDH.` → `BOTH ENDS MOVE AT ONCE.`

segments.voice: In the west, the commander was Tariq ibn Ziyad, serving under Musa ibn Nusayr, the governor of North Africa. Tariq crossed the strait, defeated the Visigothic king Roderic, and within a short time Muslim rule reached deep into the peninsula. The Arabic name for this new land was al-Andalus. In the east, the commander was Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, sent by al-Hajjaj, the harsh governor of Iraq from Hasan al-Basri's story. He took the port of Daybul and defeated King Dahir of Sindh. Call them what they were: conquests, with armies, sieges, people killed and captured. The histories that tell them were written by the winners' side, and they don't hide the fighting. But they also record what came after. The historian al-Baladhuri reports that in Sindh, when the people of Brahmanabad asked to rebuild their temples and keep their worship, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim allowed it, treating their temples like the churches and synagogues of Christians and Jews, protected in return for a tax. In al-Andalus, Christians and Jews also went on living under Muslim rule with that protected status. Over time, both places grew their own Muslim cultures: al-Andalus with its scholars and cities, Sindh as an early door through which Islam entered South Asia. An empire ruled from Damascus now touched the Atlantic and the Indus. So keep the number, but keep it whole: a year of war, and the start of long histories of neighbors. 711.
screen: `TARIQ CROSSES THE STRAIT.` · `MUHAMMAD IBN AL-QASIM IN SINDH.` · `CONQUESTS, AND WHAT CAME AFTER.` · then, large: `711.`
